title: Four weeks of Claude Opus 5.5 on the space game I shelved in 2012: a 1:1 Earth-scale planet, from a moon down to a city in one take. Here's where my time actually goes
author: Fresh-Daikon-9408
selftext:
Since I was a kid I've wanted one game: fly from planet to planet and land anywhere, on planets the true size of the Earth, with no loading screen. In 2012 I built a Unity prototype of it, an Earth-sized planet whose whole geometry is rebuilt every frame so the ship can go anywhere at any speed. It proved the idea, but making it look real would have taken a team, so it went on the shelf.

Four weeks ago I gave that code to Claude. A few prompts later the prototype was running again, and since then it has grown into a planet engine. Plate tectonics raise the ranges and build volcanic islands, rivers carve their valleys on the GPU, and a wind-driven climate decides where forests, deserts, snow and clouds go. There are three moons you can land on, and a first city with a spaceport. It's about 21,000 lines of C++ and HLSL, most of it written by Claude Opus 5.5 and some by Codex.

What surprised me is where my time goes. Writing code stopped being the bottleneck. Deciding what the engine should do, and checking that it really does it, is the job now. Every feature starts as a written spec, and one rules file holds what we've learned: when Claude gets something wrong, we fix the rule rather than the one case, so the same mistake doesn't come back.

I never accept a fix from a screenshot. For each one, Claude writes a route of viewpoints spread across the planet and I fly it myself, because a bug that hides in one place shows up in another. That's over 70 routes so far.

The assets taught me the same lesson. The shuttle and the city's buildings start from a generative 3D model and get cleaned up in Blender. Once, an automatic check declared the cleaned-up shuttle flawless. The close-ups showed glowing leather, slits in the floor, screen graphics painted on the flight stick and 30,000 intersecting faces. Since then every asset goes through close-up sheets, near, far and in wireframe, before it gets anywhere near the game.

The video is a single take, straight out of the engine. Claude wrote the shot list and drove the cinematic mode frame by frame, and I watched each version and sent back notes, seven times in two days. A shuttle takes off from one moon, swings past a second, comes down on the planet at dawn, skims a snowy ridge above a sea of clouds, climbs back into space and lands at the spaceport of a small city in the hills.

It isn't a game yet. Today you fly, land and walk around at full scale, and the game around it is the next step.

For those of you building big games with AI: where does your time actually go now? And how do you keep the model on track over weeks?

comments.author: LongjumpingEar6840
comments.body: Veramente impressionante! Ciò che No Man's Sky non è mai stato e che avrebbe dovuto essere

comments.author: javon27
comments.body:
I started my game project last week and I'm coming to similar conclusions. The first few days I was actively delegating and kept getting frustrated because nothing was looking right. This week, I switched tactics. I asked Claude Fable 5.2 if it could build my vision as a AAA game in one week. It said no, but it came up with a 7 day plan on what it could actually do.

I let it run with that plan along with all the learnings from last week. I'm more hands off, and only check in periodically to see what kind of progress it's making. The game is looking so much better because of it.

There's still a lot of work to do, and it's taking longer between each update, but the quality is so much better

https://i.redd.it/udhqucon9n2i1.jpeg

replies.author: javon27
replies.body:
To answer your second question, a few things keep it on track for me:

- Every check has to fail first. Each automated check comes with a deliberately planted bug, and if the check doesn't catch it, I don't trust it. Your "flawless" shuttle is the reason.
- Check what was built, not the plan. The plan put every house near a well, but in the built village some were 100+ m away, and the plan check never noticed.
- Held-out seeds. It tunes on five seeds, and two stay untouched until the end of the week.
-A daily journal plus handoff files, so a fresh session picks up where the last one stopped instead of carrying a huge context.

I'm stealing your "fix the rule, not the case" idea today. My lessons were scattered across commit messages, so they now live in one rules file.

comments.body: Love it. I think as models get more capable we're going to see people focusing more on the skills of a director or creative lead and develop ai specific practices. comments.author: Andress1
comments.body: Doesn't No Man's Sky do this but much better? It has 10 years of development behind them

replies.author: Fresh-Daikon-9408
replies.body: Not really. NMS planets are much smaller than Earth, someone walked halfway around one in about 12 hours. This one is 1:1 Earth scale with seamless landing, and the rendering style is completely different. Hello Games is actually doing Earth scale in a separate game, Light No Fire, still unreleased.
